question: A gastroenterology fellow is interested in the relationship between smoking and incidence of Barrett esophagus. At a departmental grand rounds she recently attended, one of the presenters claimed that smokers are only at increased risk for Barrett esophagus in the presence of acid reflux. She decides to design a retrospective cohort study to investigate the association between smoking and Barrett esophagus. After comparing 400 smokers to 400 non-smokers identified via chart review, she finds that smokers were at increased risk of Barrett esophagus at the end of a 10-year follow-up period (RR = 1.82, p < 0.001). Among patients with a history of acid reflux, there was no relationship between smoking and Barrett esophagus (p = 0.52). Likewise, no relationship was found between smoking and Barrett esophagus among patients without a history of acid reflux (p = 0.48). The results of this study are best explained by which of the following?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: Smoking -> Increased risk of Barrett esophagus -> RR = 1.82, p < 0.001 -> 90% CHAIN: Smoking + Acid reflux -> No relationship with Barrett esophagus -> p = 0.52 -> 80% CHAIN: Smoking + No acid reflux -> No relationship with Barrett esophagus -> p = 0.48 -> 80% CHAIN: Effect modification -> Best explains the relationship between smoking and Barrett esophagus in the presence or absence of acid reflux -> 90%
analysis: The results of the study suggest that the relationship between smoking and Barrett esophagus is modified by the presence of acid reflux. Smoking alone may increase the risk of Barrett esophagus, but this effect is not seen when there is a history of acid reflux. This indicates effect modification.
